- Enter the date the LOR was mailed by certified mail and attach a copy.
- When a dec page is received, name it, save it and document the policy limits. Once the liability and UM dec pages are received and the limits are confirmed by the case manager, the phase can be changed.
- If there is **no liability insurance**, add a note, for example "Hit and Run". If coverage was **denied**, add a note and attach the coverage denial letter. Add **#liabilitydenied**, **#coverage-denied** or **#UMonly**.
- If there is **med pay**, enter the amount and a note of how much med pay coverage there is. Add **#medpay**.
- Once you have the police report, update the insurance tab with the defendant and insurance information (name, address, policy number, name of the insured, adjuster information, claim number and so on).

### Meds tab

All providers need to be listed.

- **Provider name.** If you do not know the provider's name, enter "Unknown chiro" and a note explaining why. Also set a reminder to follow up with the client and get the information.
- **Treatment status:** Actively treating or Treatment complete.
- **Notes:** enter information such as the current balance or any important note. The most recent note goes at the top. Format: **date, note, initials.** *Example: 5/1/20xx, called the liability adjuster, spoke with the adjuster, who gave verbal liability limits of 25/50. (initials)*
- Add lost wages notes and save a copy of the lost wages form.
- When medical records and bills are **requested**, enter the date of the request and add a copy of the request.
- When they are **received**, add the date received and name them.
- When the **final** medical records and bills are received, enter the dates of treatment and the medical totals. **Do not enter the totals if the client is still treating and we do not have the final bill.**
- Update the treatment status.

**If the client goes to the hospital**, we request the hospital bill, the ER physician bill and the radiologist bill (if applicable). List the provider as "Unknown ER Phys" as a reminder so you do not forget.
- The hospital bills and records must be requested **once we confirm coverage**, or once we can confirm our client has UM.
- If the client was treated at the ER more than once, add each visit separately and specify the dates of service, to be sure we request both ER physician bills, both ER hospital bills and both radiologist bills. Do not add them as one: they have different dates of service, charges and account numbers, and possibly different hospitals.
- Add **#hospital**.

**Pre-settlement loans.** Any pre-settlement loan should be saved in the medicals, but **do not enter the total amount** since it is not a medical bill. Note the loan amount in the notes section and save a copy of the loan documents. Add **#loan**.

### General things to remember

- If you walk away from your desk, **lock your computer**. We need to protect clients' personal information.
- If you are out of the office, set your status in Teams so the team knows.

title: 2-Week Calls and Balance Verifications
summary: What to ask a treating client every two weeks, why every case needs an MRI, and how to verify each provider's balance, the health insurance EOB and med pay.
body:
## 2-week calls

Every two weeks during treatment, contact the client (see the *Case Phases Procedure*). If the client says they are already treating, ask how their treatment is going, and when their next appointment is. This also helps confirm they are treating consistently.

Make sure **all** providers are included and documented in the Medical section of the case system. A provider needs to be included even if the client treated at a specific location only once. We need all the **itemized** bills and medical records from each provider the client treated with. If we do not know the provider's name, enter it as "Unknown - Chiropractor" or "ER Physician - Unknown". **Every provider needs to be in the case system.**

If the client went to the ER, ask how they got there: by EMS, or did someone take them? If by EMS, request the **EMS bill**.

### When you speak with clients about treatment, ask

1. How is treatment going? Have you made every visit so far?
2. When was your last visit?
3. When is your next visit?
4. Have you had any diagnostic testing, such as MRIs, CTs or X-rays?
   - If so, where? If the client has not had an MRI, tell them it is very likely they will be referred out for one within the first 2 to 3 weeks. **Every case should have an MRI of the body parts the client complains about.** The MRIs show potential internal injuries the client might not be aware of, and they also increase the value of the case. Personal injury chiropractors know this and usually refer clients out quickly.
   - We also need to know exactly where the client had the MRI so we can request the records and bills and check whether it was a **positive MRI finding**. Positive findings help increase the value of the case. If the client has a positive finding, they are usually referred out to an orthopedic or neurology specialist, depending on the body part injured.
5. Has the doctor sent you to any other providers? (Think of situations where one clinic refers clients to see an MD at another.)
6. Send us any bills you get in the mail. Remind clients that if they have health insurance, they can and should give it to the doctors, especially if they went to the ER. (Health insurance may or may not need to be paid back, depending on whether it is an ERISA qualified plan. Health insurance companies are able to get large reductions. At the end, clients benefit financially if health insurance pays.)
7. Make sure the client knows to tell us **any time** they are sent to a different facility by doctors. Getting the health insurance EOB also helps us find out exactly where and with whom the client treated. If there is no health insurance, we need to review the medical records thoroughly, and we may also need to call the providers to check whether they have different billing.

**Remember to have the clients verify the providers.** It is VERY important that we have all providers and all itemized bills and medical records before moving the case to ready for demand. We do not want to send the demand out if we do not have all of them (unless there is an exception, such as needing to supplement, medical bills higher than the limits, or a limits issue, case by case).

## Balance verifications

Balance verifications help make sure we do not miss a provider, and let us know whether there is health insurance, possible liens, or bills sent to collections.

When verifying balances, confirm **verbally or by email**:
- Who called whom, who we spoke with, and the phone number we called.
- The **original balance** (this confirms the bill we have is the updated and accurate one).
- The **payments made, and by whom**. For example: "Health Insurance - Cigna paid $110." This also helps confirm whether the client has used health insurance. Ask for the name of the specific insurance company that paid.
- The **adjustments made**.
- The **current balance due**.

**If the account has been sent to collections or bought by a funding company**, we need the name of the new provider, the account number and the phone number. Contact the new company and verify the balance with them. This is very important so that once the case settles we send the payment to the correct provider. **The case should not move to the next phase until this is done.** If there is a special circumstance, such as needing to send the demand and supplement later, document it.

### Other things to confirm

- **Health insurance EOB.** Request it to confirm whether health insurance made payments. It also shows whether the client treated with an additional provider we may not know about. Confirm whether the plan is an **ERISA qualified plan**: the policy language tells you, or you can call the health insurance subrogation specialist. *Hint: Medicaid, Medicare, VA and railroad plans are ERISA plans and have to be paid back.*
- **Med pay EOB.** Request it to confirm that med pay has been exhausted. Confirm on all cases whether there is med pay. Some insurers show it on the dec page and others do not. If it is not on the dec page, call the UM adjuster and ask.
- **All providers.** As soon as we know the client has completed treatment, confirm all providers. You can email the client all the providers and dates of service before the case changes to Pre-Demand, to confirm we have not missed one. All providers must be on the demand so we do not settle cases for less than they are worth.
- **Call before the demand.** The attorney or case manager calls the client before sending the demand to verify information and give an update, so the client knows the process and has realistic expectations. The attorney or case manager also double-checks that the limits are correct before the demand goes out.

title: Treatment Phase Case Review
summary: The checklist for reviewing a case in the Treatment phase: insurance, meds, general information, the case manager's monthly review, Teams and the phase tracker.
body:
Treatment means that we have **confirmed all limits**, so we know what the case may be worth. The client is actively treating, we requested the hospital records (if the client treated at the hospital), and we keep constant contact with the client. Both the liability and the UM dec pages need to be received and documented by the time the case is in Treatment. The hospital records can be requested earlier if we have confirmed at least that liability was accepted, or that UM is available and the police report shows a rear-end collision or clear liability.

**Reminders**
- Add your notes in the **Case Review** bucket.
- Assign tasks outside of the buckets to the team members.
- Use your timer any time you work on a case.
- Check the shared folder to confirm the documents (dec pages, pictures, medical records) are saved both in the document bucket and in the case system.

### Things to review

**Insurance (liability, UM and health insurance)**
- Have the dec pages been received? Are they saved in the correct insurance section? There is a box for when the LOR was sent and when the dec pages were received. These boxes need to be completed.
- Have we confirmed that liability was accepted in the liability section? (The box needs to be completed as "liability accepted". This applies to liability only, not UM.)
- Are the limits entered? (Limits are entered only once we have the dec pages.)
- In the UM section, have we received the UM signed selection form? (The field for whether the UM is add-on or reduced should be completed.)
- Has med pay been confirmed?

**Meds**
- Has an MRI been done? (It needs to be done by week 4.)
- Have the hospital records, ER physician and radiologist been requested? The boxes next to each provider are checked when requested, and the request is saved under each specific provider.
- Is there a lost wages provider? Every case should have one. If the client did not lose wages, there should be a note saying no lost wages.

**General info**
- Has there been recent contact (within 2 weeks)?
- Is there a **#hospital** tag if the client treated at the hospital?
- Is there a **#MP** or **#NoMP** tag?
- Is there a police report? If there is none because the police were not called, there should be a **#nopolicereport** tag.
- Is the **statute of limitations** correct? Review the police report; for an automobile accident it should be 2 years from the date of the accident (check the state's rule).

**Case manager monthly review**
- Has the case manager reviewed the file this month? Case managers review files once a month to make sure cases are worked up correctly. There should be notes in the Case Review bucket from the case manager's review.

**Teams**
- Check the Teams section to confirm the legal assistant and case manager have been entered correctly. If not, they will not get the correct tasks. There needs to be a **green ribbon** next to the legal assistant's name, and both the legal assistant and the case manager should be set as **primary**.
- Are there pending call-back tasks? If so, how long, and has there been contact?

**Phase tracker**
- Has the phase tracker been updated with the date each phase changed and the correct person? Investigation, File Set-Up and Treatment should all be completed by the time the case is in the Treatment phase.

title: Pre-Demand Requirements
summary: The checklist a case must meet before the demand is drafted, and the order the pre-demand package is put together.
body:
**If any of the following is not complete or is missing, the demand is returned to the legal assistant until it is ready for pre-demand.**

### Checklist

- [ ] A copy of the client's ID has been saved to the file and the contact card.
- [ ] The UM dec page is saved and the limits are noted in the insurance tab. The adjuster information is updated on the contact card.
- [ ] The UM signed selection form is saved in the file.
- [ ] The liability dec page is saved and the limits are documented in the insurance tab.
- [ ] The current adjuster contact information has been confirmed by calling the adjuster. The contact card must be updated so the demand is delivered to the correct adjuster and address.
- [ ] Med pay has been exhausted, or the bills have been submitted to the med pay adjuster. The EOB has been requested. If there is no med pay, there is a note saying so, and a **#mpc** or **#nompc** tag. All med pay information is noted in the med pay bucket, including med pay checks and invoices.
- [ ] The health insurance subrogation log is saved in the file, and the reference number is noted in the insurance section. If the client has no health insurance, there is a note saying so in the health insurance section and in the health insurance bucket.
- [ ] All case expenses are noted in the Billable Expenses tab and in the activity section. Receipts are attached and named correctly in the file. **This includes checking the records portals (MRO, Chartswap and the records vendor portals), and adding the admin fee and any sign-up fee.** Save screenshots of the portals you checked, to confirm there are no pending unpaid invoices.
  - *Example:* PP $amount paid, provider name and what it is for, client's name.
  - *Example:* Invoice $amount due, provider name and what it is for, client's name.
- [ ] Lost wages forms have been received. If there are no lost wages, there is a note saying so in the medicals section.
- [ ] Examples of pain and suffering have been added to the pain and suffering bucket.
- [ ] The client has confirmed all medical providers, dates of service, lost wages, and pain and suffering examples, and they are noted in the file. If the client confirmed by email, the email is saved in the file. **Written confirmation from the client about the providers is needed.**
- [ ] ALL medical records and itemized bills have been received.
- [ ] ALL balances have been verified for each provider the client treated with. If there was a funding company or a lien, it must be noted. The following is required and is part of the balance verification: original charges, payments made and by whom, adjustments made, current balance due. **"Health insurance" is not sufficient: we must know exactly which insurance company paid** (for example Aetna, Peach State, Medicare). If we do not have this information, the balances have not been verified. Document it in the "Balance Verification / Reductions" bucket, and put a note in the memo under the specific provider whose balance you verified.
  - *Example:* #balanceverification Called (provider name), phone number you called, name of the person you spoke with, details of the conversation.
- [ ] All documents saved and named in the case system are also in the shared folder.

### Pre-demand order

Put the pre-demand together in this order:
1. Pre-demand checklist
2. Police report
3. Pictures
4. Itemized bills, in order of treatment
5. Medical records, in order of treatment, including disability slips
6. Lost wages

When all of the above is complete, scan the entire pre-demand, create a task and give it to the case manager to draft the demand. The phase should now be changed to Pre-Demand. Once the case manager drafts the demand, it goes to the attorney for review and approval.

*There are always exceptions. If there is a special circumstance where we can or should send the demand without having all bills and records, bring it to the supervisor's or attorney's attention. We are able to supplement if necessary.*

title: Procedure: How to Process Invoices
summary: How to get an invoice paid, save it and document it in billable expenses, and what to record when accounting issues the check.
body:
### Getting an invoice paid

On the invoice, **highlight the important information** so it is easy for accounting, or anyone, to read:
- patient / client name
- records from
- balance due
- invoice number
- who the check should be made payable to

Then:
1. Add a tab to the invoice with your initials, so accounting knows who to return the invoice and the check to.
2. Place the invoice in accounting's office, in the box where invoices go.
3. Email accounting a copy of the invoice and copy the file.

### Save the invoice

- Scan the invoice and upload it in the billable expenses.
- Also save a copy under the specific provider the invoice is for. *Example: an invoice for records from a hospital is saved in the Meds section under that hospital.*
- Name it in the case system and the shared folder as: **Invoice, provider name (for example the records vendor), $amount due, provider name (for example the hospital), client's name.**

### Document it in Billable Expenses

- **Type of expense:** Medical Records (this includes bills, since there is no drop-down for bills).
- **Form of payment:** Check (accounting gives you the check).
- **Amount:** the dollar amount due on the invoice.
- **Recipient:** the provider the check will be sent to, for example the records vendor.
- **Notes:** for example "Received invoice from (vendor). Scanned and saved in file. Emailed and put in accounting's box." Enter the invoice number and any special notes. Also document it in the Activity tab under Expenses.

### When accounting issues the check

Scan a copy of the check and of the invoice, and complete the documentation in the Billable Expense. Enter:
- check number
- date written
- date mailed
- mailed by

In the notes, include the address where you mailed it.

title: Withdrawal and Termination Procedure (Personal Injury)
summary: The steps to archive a case when the firm withdraws or the client terminates the firm: tags, letters, the 48-hour rule, calls, portals, notices and the phase change.
body:
### Overview

This procedure explains how to archive a case when the firm decides to withdraw, or when the client terminates the firm, on a personal injury case. Every step below is required so the case is archived properly once we no longer represent the client. It applies only to cases the firm withdraws from or is terminated on.

**When a client terminates the firm, the withdrawal letters must be sent out within 48 hours of receiving the written termination.**

### Steps

1. **Add the tag** **#terminated** or **#withdrew** in the project vitals.
2. **Case Summary.** Go to Case Summary under the filter menu and scroll to the bottom. Under **Case Withdrawal**, choose the correct option to generate the matching questions. If the firm withdrew, click "Yes" and enter the reason, enter the withdrawal date and save a copy of the withdrawal letters in the Exit bucket. Choosing a template generates the withdrawal letter. Review that the information on the letter is correct before sending it to the client.
3. **Send the letters to the client**, with copies of the withdrawal letters sent to the insurance companies and all providers. The letter to the client is sent by **regular and certified mail**. Save the certified tracking number, and the copy of the file sent to the client, in the Exit bucket.
4. **If the firm is withdrawing, call the client** to tell them verbally. Confirm the client's name and mailing address, and give them the **statute of limitations**. Confirm we will be sending the withdrawal packet to the correct address. Giving the statute of limitations lets the client know their options if they want a second opinion.
5. **Send withdrawal letters** to all insurance companies, medical providers, funding companies, the health insurance, and anyone who received a letter of representation from us. These letters do not need to go by certified mail. In some cases, such as providers we work with or adjusters, you can email or fax the letter. Save a copy of all letters and notes in the Exit bucket.
6. **Check the records portals** (the records vendors' portals) to make sure there are no pending invoices. If there are, send a message to cancel them if possible. If not, we pay the pending invoices and take it as a loss.
7. **Email the operations director and the PI supervisor**, copying the file, about why we no longer represent the client. If the firm withdrew, state the reason. If the firm was terminated, state the reason in the email, for example "Hired another attorney" or "Unknown".
8. **Update the phase tracker** with the date the case was archived and the name of the person archiving it.
9. **Change the case phase to Archive.**

**Note:** Before withdrawing from a case, check with the attorney or supervisor and get approval. Have any documentation available for review and withdrawal approval. If the reason for withdrawal is no coverage, have the no-coverage letters in writing, including the signed UM rejection form if needed.

title: Sample Personal Injury Onboarding Packet: Contract, HIPAA Authorization and Power of Attorney
summary: A sample new-client packet from a personal injury firm: the contract for legal services (fees, costs, termination, arbitration), the HIPAA medical authorization and the power of attorney to endorse settlement checks.
body:
*This is a sample personal injury onboarding packet from a Georgia personal injury firm, shown as a reference for what a new-client packet contains. The firm's name, address and attorneys' names are left out. The fees, costs and arbitration terms are that firm's own and differ from firm to firm; each firm uses its own contract. Blanks are shown as ______.*

The packet has three parts: a contract for legal services, a HIPAA medical authorization and a power of attorney.

## 1. Contract for legal services

______ (referred to from this point on as "you"), and the law firm of [Firm Name] (referred to from this point on as "we" or "us") agree that we will represent you for any and all claims resulting from your personal injury that occurred on or about ______. You authorize us to perform all services and incur all costs and expenses as we, in our sole discretion, deem appropriate with regard to this representation.

You agree that at this point no other attorney or law firm is representing you in this claim. In addition, you have told us about any lawyers you may have hired and dismissed previously on this claim.

We agree to represent you in your claim for damages up to the point at which a judgment is entered by the court. If you do not agree with the court's judgment and wish to appeal, we are not required to represent you in the appeal. We may, but you must draw up a new agreement with us first. If you need other legal work while your damages claim is proceeding, you must draw up a separate agreement with us to do that legal work; only your damages claim is covered in this contract.

### Fees

We will be paid according to the following formula:

- We will receive **30%** of the gross (before anything is deducted) amount we recover for you **before a lawsuit is filed**.
- If we agree that filing a lawsuit is necessary, and we recover money for you **after the suit is filed**, we will receive **40%** of the gross amount we recover.
- You agree to assign us a **lien** (that is, admit that we have a legal right to pursue collection) against any money that is recovered or that may be recovered based on our handling of the claim.

If we believe that you have a legitimate claim and that recovery of money for damages is likely, we will pay up front any costs involved in proceeding with your claim, such as travel, fees for copying records, court costs, and the like. Any expenses we have already paid or are obligated to pay in proceeding with your claim will be reimbursed to us out of your share of the money recovered by settlement or judgment, plus a $250.00 administrative fee.

**IF THERE IS NO RECOVERY, WE WILL RECEIVE NO FEE. IF THERE IS NO RECOVERY, CLIENT SHALL NOT BE RESPONSIBLE FOR ANY OF OUR COSTS AND EXPENSES.**

We agree to do our best to obtain everything to which you are properly entitled. However, we cannot predict what the outcome will be and do not promise you any particular result or dollar amount of compensation.

### Other counsel, settlement advice and ending the representation

Client agrees that Attorneys may associate other counsel to assist in this representation. If other counsel is associated, Client agrees that Attorneys may divide the total attorney fees based on the sole judgment of Attorneys without further notice to or consent of Client, so long as such division of fees is in accord with rules governing the conduct of Attorneys.

If we tell you that a settlement offer you have received is a good one and you should accept it, and you refuse to take our advice, we will have the right to withdraw from continuing to represent you.

You have the right at any time to provide us with written notice that you do not wish for us to continue to represent you. However, if you dismiss us, we may charge you for the value of the time we have spent in proceeding with your claim, based on the following:

- $350/hour for all billable hours by attorneys.
- $100/hour for all billable hours by non-attorney staff.
- Full out-of-pocket costs that may have been incurred, such as court filing fees, sheriff's fees, deposition costs, photocopying, medical records requests fee, etc.

If termination occurs with an offer pending, or after settlement or verdict, Attorneys shall be entitled to their full percentage of the recovery as provided in the attorney fee section above, it being agreed that those fees were earned.

### Disputes

Client has read this Contract and any questions have been addressed to Client's satisfaction. Any dispute arising under this agreement will be submitted to arbitration in Atlanta, Georgia under the rules and procedures of the State Bar of Georgia Committee on the Arbitration of Attorney Fee Disputes, if concerning fees, or by an arbitrator to be agreed to by the parties, if concerning any other matter. Alternatively, you may choose to arbitrate any dispute arising under this agreement in Atlanta by a single arbitrator provided through the Atlanta office of Judicial Arbitration and Mediation Service ("JAMS"). The decision of any such arbitrator or arbitrators shall be binding, conclusive, and not appealable. In the event a dispute is not or cannot be arbitrated, the parties consent to the jurisdiction of and venue in the courts of Gwinnett County, Georgia.

If we do not receive a signed copy of this contract within 5 days, we will assume that you have obtained other counsel, and shall mark our file "closed" and do nothing further.

**WE HAVE READ AND UNDERSTAND THE FOLLOWING CONTRACT AND AGREE TO ABIDE BY WHAT IT SAYS.**

Signatures: ______ (Client) ______ (Date); ______ (Attorney) ______ (Date)

## 2. HIPAA-compliant medical authorization for release / disclosure of protected health information (pursuant to 45 CFR 164.508)

TO: ______ I authorize and request the disclosure of all protected information for the purpose of review and evaluation in connection with a legal claim. I expressly request that the designated records custodian of all covered entities under HIPAA identified above disclose full and complete protected medical information.

- Patient's full name: ______
- Date of birth: ______   Social Security: ______
- Current address: ______
- Date of service being requested: ______

This authorization shall be in force and effect until two (2) years from the date of execution, at which time the authorization expires.

This authorization applies to: ALL MEDICAL RECORDS [ ]   ITEMIZED BILL [ ]

You are authorized to release the information being requested to any representative of [Firm Name], or send it to the firm's address, fax or email shown on the form.

Purpose of use / disclosure: **LEGAL**   Information to be used / disclosed: **LEGAL**

I understand that the information used or disclosed pursuant to this authorization may be subject to re-disclosure and may then no longer be protected by the Federal Privacy Regulations. I understand that, unless otherwise limited by state or federal regulations, I may revoke this authorization at any time by presenting my revocation in writing, to the extent that the entity identified above has acted in reliance on this authorization, a revocation form may be obtained from the medical records department; the completed revocation must be presented to the medical records department. I further understand that this authorization is specific to the information checked above, for the date(s) of service indicated, and for the purpose written above.

I understand that my treatment or payment for my treatment cannot be conditioned on the signing of this form. I also understand that the information released in response to this authorization may be re-disclosed to other parties.

I understand the information to be released or disclosed may include information relating to sexually transmitted diseases, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and alcohol and drug abuse. I authorize the release or disclosure of this type of information.

Signature of patient or legally authorized representative: ______ Date: ______
Name of patient or legally authorized representative: ______ Relationship: ______

## 3. Power of attorney

STATE OF GEORGIA, COUNTY OF ______

KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS: That I, ______, a resident of ______ County, State of Georgia, being desirous of arranging for the transaction of my business through an attorney in fact, have appointed, named and constituted, and by these presents do name, constitute and appoint the firm's named attorneys and the law firm of [Firm Name] as my true and lawful attorney in fact, and do authorize said attorney in fact, for me, and in my name, place and stead, to **sign, endorse and deposit checks related to my case.**

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand and affixed my seal, today's date: ______

Signature: ______   Witness / Notary: ______
Sworn and subscribed to me this ____ of ______ 20__. My commission expires on ______.

title: What happens after a car accident in Florida? The property damage claim process
summary: The six steps of a property damage claim after a car accident: intake, liability, insurance and coverage, vehicle damage, repair or total loss, and final documentation, with what is gathered and the skill used at each step.
body:
*A simple guide to the property damage portion of a car accident claim, and how the information you collect is used at each stage. It is written for Florida; the same steps apply in most states, but the rules and forms differ, so confirm anything unclear with the handling attorney.*

When a car accident happens, several key steps are taken to evaluate, document and resolve the property damage portion of the claim. This page walks through those steps in order.

## The six steps at a glance

| Step | The question it answers | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Intake** | What happened? | Collect the essential details and open the property damage claim. |
| **2. Liability** | Who may be responsible? | The adjuster reviews the evidence; you keep the facts organized and the claim coordinated. |
| **3. Insurance and coverage** | Which insurance applies? | Verify the policies and what they cover. |
| **4. Vehicle damage** | How much will it cost to repair? | Document the damage and get a repair estimate. |
| **5. Repair or total loss** | Can the vehicle be repaired? | Follow the repair process or the total loss process. |
| **6. Documentation and follow-up** | What is needed to finalize the claim? | Collect the final documents and keep the file moving. |

## 1. Intake: what happened?

We begin by collecting the essential details about the accident to open the property damage claim.

**Key information gathered:**

- Your vehicle information
- Parties involved
- Details of how the accident happened
- Police or accident report
- Insurance information (your policy and the other party's)
- Photos and any available documentation

**Skill highlight:** information gathering, organization and claim setup.

## 2. Liability: who may be responsible?

After the claim is submitted, the insurance company assigns an adjuster to investigate and determine liability based on the available evidence.

**Factors reviewed:**

- Your version of the accident
- The other driver's version
- The police report narrative
- Photos of the vehicles and damages
- Damage locations and patterns
- Other supporting documentation

**Skill highlight:** fact organization and claim coordination.

## 3. Insurance and coverage: which insurance applies?

The claim involves reviewing the relevant insurance policies and coverage that may apply to the property damage.

**Coverage that may be involved:**

- Your policy (for example, collision coverage and deductible considerations)
- The other driver's property damage liability coverage
- Policy limits and coverage details
- Any additional applicable coverage

**Skill highlight:** insurance verification and coverage coordination.

## 4. Vehicle damage: how much will it cost to repair?

Once coverage and liability issues are addressed, the vehicle damage is documented and evaluated.

**Damage evaluation includes:**

- Vehicle photographs
- A virtual estimate or an in-person inspection
- A repair estimate prepared by an appraiser or authorized source
- Review of visible and related damages

**Skill highlight:** damage documentation and repair coordination.

## 5. Repair or total loss: can the vehicle be repaired?

Based on the estimate and the extent of the damages, the claim will follow either a repair process or a total loss process.

| | **Repair process** | **Total loss process** |
|---|---|---|
| **When** | If repairable | If considered a total loss |
| **What happens** | Schedule repairs at a repair facility. Rental vehicle may be provided (if applicable). Repairs are completed and the vehicle is returned to you. | The vehicle's value is evaluated. The total loss process is initiated. Settlement and next steps depend on the policy, the damages and other circumstances. |

**Skill highlight:** case analysis and repair or total loss coordination.

## 6. Documentation and follow-up: what is needed to finalize the claim?

After repairs are completed (or the total loss process is resolved), final documents are collected and the claim is updated accordingly.

**Final documentation may include:**

- Property damage estimate
- Photos of the vehicle
- Repair invoices
- Proof of payment
- Rental information (if applicable)
- Any additional claim-related documentation

**Skill highlight:** case management and follow-through to keep the file moving.

## The takeaway

Behind every property damage claim is a process of gathering information, verifying coverage, coordinating with insurers, documenting damage and keeping the file moving.

## Terms to know

These are in the Glossary: **Property Damage (PD), Collision Coverage, Deductible, Policy Limits, Total Loss, Diminished Value, Loss of Use, First-Party Claim, Third-Party Claim, Adjuster.**

title: How to calculate non-economic damages
summary: What pain and suffering and the other non-economic damages are, how a value is built step by step (multiplier, per diem, evaluation software, comparable verdicts), what raises or lowers it, and what to gather to support it.
body:
*A guide for case managers, medical summary writers and demand staff. There is no formula in the law for pain and suffering, and the rules differ by state and by court. Use this as a framework to understand how a number is built and what to gather to support it, and confirm every figure and every legal rule with the handling attorney. The attorney sets the value of a case, not the support team.*

## 1. What non-economic damages are

When a person is hurt because of someone else's carelessness, the law lets them recover **damages**: money to make up for the harm. Damages fall into two main groups.

| | **Economic damages (special damages)** | **Non-economic damages (general damages)** |
|---|---|---|
| **What they cover** | Losses with a bill, a pay stub or a receipt | Losses that have no price tag, because they are about how the injury changed the person's life |
| **Examples** | Medical bills, future medical care, lost wages, lost earning capacity, property damage, out-of-pocket costs | Pain and suffering, mental anguish, loss of enjoyment of life, scarring, physical impairment, loss of companionship |
| **How the amount is found** | Add up the documents | Judgment, supported by evidence |
| **Typical proof** | Bills, records, wage statements, estimates | Medical records, photos, the client's own account, statements from family, friends and co-workers |

**Punitive damages** are a third, separate category. They punish especially bad conduct and are rare in ordinary injury claims, so they are not part of this page.

### The main kinds of non-economic loss

| Kind of loss | What it means in real life |
|---|---|
| **Pain and suffering** | Physical pain, soreness, stiffness, headaches, the discomfort of treatment, injections and surgery, and the pain that continues afterwards. |
| **Mental anguish and emotional distress** | Fear, anxiety, depression, trouble sleeping, flashbacks, fear of driving, and the stress of a long recovery. |
| **Loss of enjoyment of life** (sometimes called hedonic damages) | Not being able to do the things that make up a good life: playing with the kids, sports, gardening, travel, church, hobbies, even a full night's sleep. |
| **Disfigurement and scarring** | Visible scars, burns or changes to appearance, and the embarrassment that comes with them. |
| **Physical impairment or disability** | Permanent loss of movement, strength or function, and the limits it puts on everyday tasks. |
| **Loss of consortium** | A spouse's own claim for the loss of companionship, help and intimacy caused by the partner's injury. |
| **Inconvenience and humiliation** | Needing help with bathing or dressing, giving up independence, and the indignity of it. |

Non-economic damages are usually described in two parts: **past** (from the accident to today, or to trial) and **future** (for the rest of the person's life, if the injury is permanent). A demand often values the two separately.

## 2. Why there is no exact number, and what the support team's job is

A bill has an amount on it. Pain does not. A jury, or an adjuster guessing what a jury would do, has to turn the effect of an injury on a person's life into dollars. Courts do not give a formula for this, so the methods below are **tools for negotiation and for explaining a figure**. They are not rules of law.

For the support team, the job is **not** to put a value on the case. The job is to:

- **Gather and organize** the evidence that shows how the injury affected the person: medical records, bills, photos, statements.
- **Build the medical chronology** so the attorney can see the pain, the treatment and the recovery in order.
- **Check the numbers**: totals, dates, duplicates, unpaid bills, anything that does not belong to this accident.
- **Flag risks**: treatment gaps, a prior injury to the same body part, inconsistent histories, a long wait before the first visit.
- **Draft what the attorney asks for**, such as the damages section of the demand, and let the attorney decide the figure.

**Never** quote a case value, a range or a "typical" settlement to a client, an adjuster or anyone else unless the attorney has told you to. Clients remember numbers.

## 3. How a value is built, step by step

1. **Verify the economic damages.** Add up the medical bills, lost wages and other costs, using only items related to this accident. This is the base for most methods.
2. **Understand the injury.** What was injured, how badly, and how long did it last? Was there surgery, injections, a hospital stay, a fracture, a head injury, a scar, a permanent restriction?
3. **Check permanency.** Did a doctor say the problem is permanent, give an impairment rating or describe future care? This is often the biggest single driver of value.
4. **Pick the method (or two).** The attorney chooses. Running two methods and comparing is common, so one number does not stand on its own.
5. **Adjust for the case itself.** Strength of liability, the client's share of fault, the venue, the policy limits and whether the at-fault party can pay.
6. **Set a range.** Attorneys usually think in a range: the lowest figure the client would accept, a target, and an opening demand.
7. **Write the reasoning down.** In the demand, the figure is supported by a story and evidence. A number without a reason is easy to dismiss.

## 4. The common methods

### 4.1 The multiplier method

The medical bills (and sometimes lost wages as well) are multiplied by a number, often between about **1.5 and 5**. The multiplier is higher when the injury is more serious, permanent, supported by objective findings and the other side clearly caused the accident. It is lower when treatment was short, the injury healed, or there are problems with the evidence.

**Example A: a neck and back injury that healed after four months.**

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Medical bills | $12,000 |
| Lost wages | $2,500 |
| Multiplier on medical bills | 2.5 |
| **Non-economic damages** ($12,000 × 2.5) | **$30,000** |
| **Total** ($12,000 + $2,500 + $30,000) | **$44,500** |

If the attorney applies the multiplier to bills **and** wages together, the result is: ($12,000 + $2,500) × 2.5 = $36,250 non-economic, and a total of $14,500 + $36,250 = **$50,750**.

**Example B: a broken leg that needed surgery, with a lasting limp.**

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Medical bills | $85,000 |
| Lost wages | $20,000 |
| Multiplier on medical bills | 4 |
| **Non-economic damages** ($85,000 × 4) | **$340,000** |
| **Total** ($85,000 + $20,000 + $340,000) | **$445,000** |

The total is a starting point for negotiation. The most the insurer can pay is limited by the policy limits, and the client's own share of fault, if any, reduces it.

**Watch out for:**

- The multiplier is a **rule of thumb**, not a law, and insurers do not all use it.
- It rewards large medical bills. A serious injury with little treatment (for example, someone who could not afford care) looks smaller under this method than it is.
- In some states only the amount actually **paid** or owed for treatment can be shown to a jury, not the full amount billed. That changes the base the multiplier is applied to.

### 4.2 The per diem method

"Per diem" means "per day". A dollar amount is given to each day of pain and multiplied by the number of days.

**Example: the same neck and back injury.**

| Period | Rate | Days | Amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active treatment | $120 a day | 150 | $18,000 |
| Lingering pain after treatment ended | $40 a day | 365 | $14,600 |
| **Total (past)** | | | **$32,600** |

For a **permanent** injury the per diem can be extended over the person's **life expectancy**, taken from published life tables. For example, $25 a day for 20 years is $25 × 365 × 20 = **$182,500**. Whether future amounts are reduced to their present value varies by state.

**Watch out for:**

- Choosing the daily rate is the hard part. Some attorneys tie it to something a jury can relate to, such as what a fair day's pay would be for putting up with the pain.
- Some courts do not let a lawyer suggest a per diem figure to a jury. The attorney will know the local rule.
- It works best when the period of pain is clear. It is a poor fit if the dates of treatment are unclear or there are long gaps.

### 4.3 Claims evaluation software

Many insurance companies run injury claims through **evaluation software** (Colossus is a well-known one). The adjuster enters the type of injury, the treatment, the length of care, the effect on work and other facts, and the program suggests a range. This is why the **way an injury is described and coded in the medical records matters**: specific diagnoses, objective findings and consistent notes tend to score higher than general complaints.

### 4.4 Comparable verdicts and settlements

Attorneys compare the case with **similar injuries** that ended in verdicts or settlements in the same area. Age, injury, treatment, permanency and venue all matter. This is research and judgment, and it is the method most likely to reflect what a jury in that court would actually do.

### 4.5 Quick comparison

| Method | How it works | Best for | Main weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Multiplier** | Medical bills × a number | Everyday injury claims with documented treatment | Depends on the size of the bills; the multiplier is a guess |
| **Per diem** | Daily rate × days of pain | Injuries with a clear start and end, and permanent injuries over a lifetime | The daily rate is arbitrary; some courts do not allow it |
| **Evaluation software** | Points for injury, treatment, and other inputs | Understanding what an insurer is likely to offer | Depends on how well the file is documented |
| **Comparable verdicts** | Similar cases in the same area | Serious or unusual cases | Hard to find truly similar cases |

## 5. What raises or lowers the value

| Tends to raise the value | Tends to lower the value |
|---|---|
| Surgery, fractures, a head or spinal injury, scarring | A minor injury that resolved quickly |
| A doctor's opinion that the injury is permanent, with an impairment rating | No permanency opinion |
| Objective findings: MRI or CT results, x-rays, test results | Complaints with no objective findings |
| Consistent care from the first visit onward | A long delay before the first visit, or gaps in treatment |
| Clear effect on work, sleep, family life and hobbies, shown by evidence | Little or no evidence of how daily life changed |
| A sympathetic, credible client with a clean history | Inconsistent statements, social media posts that contradict the claim |
| Clear fault on the other side, strong evidence of how it happened | Disputed fault, or a share of fault on the client |
| High policy limits, or a defendant who can pay | Low limits and no other source of recovery |
| A venue that tends to be generous to injured people | A venue that tends to be conservative |
| Younger age at injury (a longer life with the injury) | Prior injuries or conditions in the same body part (the other side will blame them) |

Two of these deserve a closer look.

**Treatment gaps.** A gap in care lets the insurer argue the person got better, or that the pain was not serious. If a gap exists, find out why (cost, work, family, a provider closing, the person was waiting on an approval) and make sure it is explained in the file. See the page on handling treatment gaps in the demand phase.

**Pre-existing conditions.** A prior injury or condition does not end the claim. The law generally lets a person recover for an **aggravation** of a prior condition, but the demand has to show what the person was like **before** and what is different **now**. Collect the older records so the comparison is based on facts rather than guesses.

## 6. Limits and special rules that change the number

These vary a great deal by state. Check with the attorney on the rule that applies to the case.

- **Comparative fault.** If the client is partly at fault, the total award, including non-economic damages, is reduced by the client's percentage. Some states bar recovery if the client is more than half at fault, and a few bar it if the client is even slightly at fault.
- **No-fault thresholds.** In a no-fault state, the right to claim pain and suffering from the at-fault driver in a car accident is limited unless the injury meets a **threshold**. Florida is a common example: the injury generally has to be a permanent injury (or involve significant scarring or disfigurement, or death) before non-economic damages can be claimed from the at-fault driver. Other states use terms such as "serious injury" or "serious impairment". In these states, **a doctor's opinion on permanency is central to the case**.
- **Caps.** Some states cap non-economic damages in certain kinds of cases (medical malpractice and claims against the government are the most common), and a few have wider caps. Caps are state-specific, and some have been struck down by courts.
- **Policy limits.** A claim can be worth more than the money available. Check the limits early.
- **Liens and reductions.** What the client takes home is affected by liens and fees, but those do not change the value of the claim itself. Keep them separate when you write about damages.

## 7. What to gather to support non-economic damages

This is the support team's checklist. The more specific and the more dated the evidence is, the better it supports the number.

**Medical**

- [ ] Complete medical records and bills from every provider
- [ ] Imaging reports and, where requested, the images
- [ ] A medical chronology or summary showing dates, complaints, pain levels, treatment and progress
- [ ] A doctor's report or narrative on **permanency, impairment rating, work and activity restrictions and future care**
- [ ] A future care estimate, such as a recommended surgery or ongoing therapy, with the expected cost
- [ ] Mental health treatment records, if any, and records of medication for pain, anxiety or sleep

**Photos and records of the injury**

- [ ] Photos of injuries at the start, during healing and now, including scars, bruises, casts and braces
- [ ] Photos of the vehicles or the scene, if they show the force of the impact

**The person's own account**

- [ ] A pain journal or diary: what hurts, how much, and what the person could not do that day
- [ ] The client's own description of life before and after the accident

**Statements from other people**

- [ ] Short statements from family, friends, co-workers or a supervisor describing the person before and after
- [ ] An employer letter on missed work, light duty or a change in duties
- [ ] Records of activities given up: team rosters, gym or class memberships, travel plans cancelled

**The baseline**

- [ ] Earlier records for the same body part, so the "before" is accurate

## 8. The non-economic damages in the demand

The damages section of the demand usually does three things:

1. **Lists the economic damages** with exact totals and where each number comes from.
2. **Tells the story of the non-economic harm** in specific, human detail: the date of the accident, what the first weeks were like, what the person could no longer do, what the doctors said about the future. "The client could not lift her two-year-old for six weeks" does more than "the client experienced pain and suffering".
3. **States the demand figure**, as the attorney decides, with the reasoning behind it.

Keep the tone factual. Avoid exaggeration, because anything an adjuster can disprove weakens the rest of the demand. See also the pages in this library on writing a demand letter and on the pre-demand requirements.

## 9. Common mistakes

- **Treating a method as the law.** A multiplier or per diem is a way of explaining a figure. Do not present it as the rule.
- **Quoting a number to the client** or to the adjuster without the attorney's approval.
- **Including bills that do not belong**: unrelated treatment, duplicates, or charges from before the accident.
- **Missing the permanency opinion.** In many states this decides whether non-economic damages can be claimed at all.
- **Ignoring treatment gaps** instead of explaining them.
- **Thin evidence of daily life.** A demand with ten pages of bills and no description of how the person's life changed leaves money on the table.
- **Counting the same loss twice**, such as lost wages inside a pain and suffering figure.
- **Mixing in liens, fees and take-home amounts** when describing damages.
- **Forgetting future care and future loss** for an injury that is expected to last.

## 10. Terms to know
